title: Technical deep dive - Audit Log Export (Splunk/S3/Webhook)
topics: SIEM integration expectations; Splunk HEC vs S3 export vs webhook; delivery lag requirements; retry/backpressure and dead-lettering; ordering/idempotency; filtering and RBAC for export configuration; formats/partitioning and encryption; operational visibility (metrics/alerts); data residency and retention.
summary: StratusPay walked through their audit log ingestion patterns (Splunk Cloud + an S3-based security lake) and asked detailed questions about Redwood's export mechanisms: transport options (Splunk HEC, S3, generic webhook), expected delivery latency, failure handling (retries, DLQ, replay), and how to correlate events back to user actions (request_id, actor attribution). Redwood described the audit log pipeline (ingest/validate/store/export), at-least-once delivery semantics, per-sink backoff and dead-letter behavior, and suggested patterns for webhook signing + idempotent consumption. Customer emphasized they need near-real-time signals for privileged actions (RBAC/API key changes) and auditor-friendly retention/export controls. Next steps were to send a sample JSONL export (schema v1), confirm Splunk HEC specifics, and align on delivery lag SLO and replay expectations for their procurement/security review.
questions: Does Redwood support Splunk HEC directly or only generic webhook?; Can we export to customer-owned S3 with KMS and required prefixes/partitions?; What are the retry semantics and how do you prevent duplicates?; Is ordering guaranteed per org or per actor?; Can we filter exports to only sensitive events or specific namespaces?; What is the delivery lag SLO and how do we get alerted?; Can we replay/export historical windows if Splunk is down?; How is the export configuration itself audited?; How do you handle IP/user-agent and any privacy redaction constraints?
action_items: Svetlana Petrenko (Redwood) - Send StratusPay a sample export payload (JSONL) for audit event schema v1 + field glossary (actor/target/outcome/request_id) - due 2025-06-30
Chloe Martin (Redwood) - Confirm current Console Audit Logs API export endpoints and rate limits for listing/export configuration - due 2025-07-01
Kevin Osei (Redwood) - Share exporter failure-handling notes (retry/backoff, DLQ, replay options) and recommended consumer idempotency approach - due 2025-07-01
Jon Carver (StratusPay) - Provide Splunk Cloud HEC requirements (token auth, TLS settings, expected sourcetype/index, max event size) - due 2025-06-30
Mina Patel (StratusPay) - Provide target delivery lag requirement for P0 privileged events and acceptable duplicate rate/handling - due 2025-07-02
next_steps: Redwood to email sample schema v1 events + export examples (S3 + webhook) and proposed SLO language.
Customer to confirm preferred sink for beta (Splunk HEC vs S3) and whether they need both concurrently.
Schedule a follow-up (30 min) to validate Splunk HEC details and walk through replay/DLQ operations.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Technical deep dive - Audit Log Export (Splunk/S3/Webhook)
Date: 2025-06-26
Start time: 10:30 AM PT
Duration: 57 minutes

Attendees
- Liam O'Rourke (Redwood Inference)
- Svetlana Petrenko (Redwood Inference)
- Kevin Osei (Redwood Inference)
- Chloe Martin (Redwood Inference)
- Mina Patel (StratusPay)
- Jon Carver (StratusPay)
- Elena Ruiz (StratusPay)
- Samir Qureshi (StratusPay)

---
Auto Summary (generated)
- Customer uses Splunk Cloud and an internal S3 security data lake.
- They need reliable, near-real-time export of sensitive admin actions.
- Discussion focused on delivery semantics, retry/DLQ, replay, and formats.

Topics
1) Sinks: Splunk HEC, S3, Webhook
2) Latency + delivery lag SLO
3) Failure handling: retries, backpressure, DLQ
4) Duplicates/idempotency + ordering
5) Filtering + export configuration RBAC
6) Formats (JSONL), compression, partitioning
7) Security: signing, TLS/mTLS, KMS

Action items
- (see Action Items section above)

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for jumping on. This is the technical deep dive specifically on audit log export. Mina, Jon, Elena, Samir—anything you want to make sure we hit, like top three?

[00:13] Mina Patel: Yeah. Top is: can we get this into Splunk without building a bunch of glue. Second is latency. We need, like, near real time for privileged actions. And third is what happens when something breaks—like does it queue, does it drop, can we replay.

[00:31] Jon Carver: And I want to understand S3 too. We have a lake pattern where we land security events into S3 with KMS, partitions by day, and then we run detection jobs. Splunk is for SOC, but S3 is for longer retention.

[00:46] Liam O'Rourke: Got it. Svetlana owns SIEM/export integrations on our side, Kevin covers retention/redaction controls, Chloe is on the Console API side. I’ll mostly facilitate.

[00:58] Svetlana Petrenko: Hey everyone.

[00:59] Chloe Martin: Hi.

[01:01] Kevin Osei: Hey.

[01:03] Elena Ruiz: Hi.

[01:04] Samir Qureshi: Hey.

[01:06] Liam O'Rourke: Cool. Svetlana, want to start with what we support today and what’s on the immediate roadmap?

[01:14] Svetlana Petrenko: Sure. So, high level: audit logs get generated across services—console actions, API key operations, RBAC changes, deployment rollouts—and they go through a pipeline where we validate against a schema, persist to an internal store, and then optionally export to customer-controlled destinations.

[01:34] Svetlana Petrenko: For destinations, the ones we’re actively supporting are S3 export and webhook. For Splunk specifically, we can do Splunk HEC as a first-class sink for some customers, but under the hood it behaves like a webhook with Splunk-specific batching and headers.

[01:52] Mina Patel: When you say “webhook,” is that like we host an endpoint and you post events as they happen?

[01:57] Svetlana Petrenko: Exactly. HTTPS POST, JSON payload. We can do per-event or micro-batch. Most customers prefer micro-batch for throughput and to avoid hammering the endpoint.

[02:10] Jon Carver: What’s “micro batch” like—10 events, 100 events?

[02:15] Svetlana Petrenko: Configurable. We typically default to something like up to 100 events or up to, say, 1MB, whichever comes first. The limit is partly to avoid Splunk HEC max size issues and general proxy limits.

[02:31] Elena Ruiz: For Splunk Cloud, we use HEC. There’s also the indexer acknowledgment thing. Do you support that?

[02:38] Svetlana Petrenko: Good question. Splunk HEC has an ack feature where Splunk gives you an ack ID and then you poll. We do not rely on polling-based acknowledgements today. We treat the HTTP 200/202 from HEC as accepted.

[02:54] Elena Ruiz: That means potentially accepted but not indexed, right.

[02:57] Svetlana Petrenko: Yeah, that’s a known nuance. For most SOC workflows, “accepted by HEC” is enough. If you require end-to-end “indexed” confirmation, we’d need to add the ack polling. It’s doable but adds complexity/latency. We can track it as a requirement.

[03:15] Mina Patel: Okay. Put a pin in that. Let’s talk latency. What’s the typical delivery time from action to export?

[03:22] Svetlana Petrenko: So, we track delivery lag as the difference between event time and time it’s exported. Internally we target a 99th percentile within single-digit minutes for exports. For non-export, just availability in the Console is usually faster.

[03:41] Jon Carver: Single digit minutes is vague. Our SOC wants like under 2 minutes ideally, for P0 actions. Like API key created, RBAC change, org admin added.

[03:52] Kevin Osei: Just to clarify, are you saying “detect within 2 minutes,” or “arrive in Splunk within 2 minutes”? Because some customers do a two-stage—console for immediate triage, SIEM for correlation.

[04:04] Mina Patel: Arrive in Splunk within 2 minutes for critical ones, yeah.

[04:09] Svetlana Petrenko: That’s helpful. We can likely get close on average. The main causes of tail latency are backpressure at the sink (like Splunk HEC returning 503 or rate limiting), or if there’s a regional backlog.

[04:26] Chloe Martin: Also, it depends on filtering. If you export everything including non-sensitive events, volume can spike. But if you export only sensitive actions, it’s a smaller stream.

[04:36] Jon Carver: Do you let us filter by type? Like only rbac.* or api_key.* events.

[04:42] Chloe Martin: Yes. The export configuration supports event namespaces and/or explicit allowlists of event names. You can say “only export the sensitive set,” or “only export these namespaces.”

[04:57] Mina Patel: How do we know you’re not missing events? Like if a developer adds a new privileged action and forgets to add audit log export.

[05:05] Kevin Osei: That’s part of what we’re standardizing right now—there’s a sensitive actions inventory and we enforce coverage. For the customer-facing contract, we usually define the set of sensitive actions covered and maintain it versioned.

[05:20] Samir Qureshi: From compliance perspective, we’ll need to show auditors that privileged operations are logged and retained. The “versioned list” helps.

[05:30] Liam O'Rourke: Yeah, and for your procurement package, we can provide the list of events we guarantee in the current release, plus how we handle schema evolution.

[05:41] Elena Ruiz: On schema evolution—do you break fields? Like rename stuff?

[05:46] Chloe Martin: The schema has a version field. We try to keep backward compatibility within a major version. We can add fields, but we don’t remove required fields. Renames would be done via dual-write and deprecation window.

[06:02] Jon Carver: Okay. Let’s go into S3 export. Is it writing objects into our bucket, or do we pull?

[06:09] Svetlana Petrenko: We support push to your bucket. You create a bucket and role/policy that allows us to write. We can support SSE-KMS with your CMK. We write compressed JSON lines.

[06:24] Jon Carver: Partitions? Like prefix by date?

[06:27] Svetlana Petrenko: Typically it’s like s3://bucket/redwood-audit/org_id=.../year=2025/month=06/day=26/hour=10/…

[06:39] Jon Carver: That’s good.

[06:41] Mina Patel: And encryption in transit is TLS, obviously.

[06:45] Svetlana Petrenko: Yep.

[06:46] Mina Patel: For cross-account role, we prefer an external ID.

[06:50] Svetlana Petrenko: We can provide an external ID, yes.

[06:54] Elena Ruiz: For Splunk, do you support IP allowlisting? Splunk Cloud is weird because egress and ingress IPs can be dynamic.

[07:02] Svetlana Petrenko: For webhook delivery, we can originate from a stable set of egress IPs per region, and we can share those. For Splunk Cloud, you typically allowlist our IPs on your side if you have a gateway in front. If you can’t allowlist, we can also do mTLS in some deployments, but that’s not default.

[07:22] Mina Patel: We can front with an API gateway, probably.

[07:25] Liam O'Rourke: Elena, are you using Splunk’s HEC endpoint directly, or do you proxy through something?

[07:30] Elena Ruiz: We proxy through an internal gateway so we can do some validation and enrichments.

[07:35] Liam O'Rourke: Great, then IP allowlisting is workable.

[07:39] Mina Patel: Failure modes: say Splunk is down or rate limiting. What do you do?

[07:46] Svetlana Petrenko: The exporter will retry with exponential backoff. We also have backpressure handling so if the sink is slow, we queue and process later. We do not intentionally drop audit logs.

[08:01] Mina Patel: “Queue” where? Like for how long.

[08:06] Svetlana Petrenko: Internally we have a durable queue. The retention of that queue is configurable based on your plan, but the idea is we can sustain outages and then catch up.

[08:18] Jon Carver: If it’s down for, say, 12 hours, do you still have everything?

[08:22] Svetlana Petrenko: In most cases, yes, provided you’re within the queue retention window and volume isn’t extreme. We can also do replay from persisted audit log storage, but replay is not “automatic” unless configured.

[08:37] Elena Ruiz: Can we manually trigger replay? Like “re-send from 8 AM to 10 AM.”

[08:43] Chloe Martin: There’s not a self-serve “replay window” button in the UI today, but we can support it via support/ops. We’re working on a more self-serve export job concept.

[08:57] Mina Patel: Okay, so in beta we might need to work with support.

[09:00] Liam O'Rourke: That’s fair. We can document that in the runbook.

[09:06] Samir Qureshi: From audit/compliance, we’ll ask: how do you prove events weren’t altered and weren’t lost.

[09:13] Kevin Osei: We can talk about tamper resistance. The internal store is append-only semantics and access is restricted. For export, it’s at-least-once delivery, meaning duplicates are possible but losses are not expected. We can provide metrics on exported count vs persisted count.

[09:33] Jon Carver: Duplicates are a problem for Splunk licensing, though. And detection rules might double fire.

[09:40] Svetlana Petrenko: Yeah. At-least-once means you should treat the events as idempotent. Each event has a stable event_id, and you can de-dup on ingest. Splunk can do that via props/transforms or in your gateway.

[09:54] Elena Ruiz: What’s the ID called? Like “id”?

[09:57] Svetlana Petrenko: In schema v1 it’s event_id, plus request_id for correlation.

[10:04] Mina Patel: Ordering. Do you guarantee ordering? Like, role updated then role deleted, etc.

[10:11] Chloe Martin: We don’t guarantee global ordering across all events. We can provide ordering within a partition (like per org) in the store, but export concurrency can reorder. The recommended approach is treat each event independently and rely on timestamps plus event_id.

[10:30] Jon Carver: That’s acceptable.

[10:32] Mina Patel: About the sensitive actions: do you include diffs? Like, if RBAC policy changed, I need who changed what.

[10:39] Chloe Martin: For RBAC changes we include a diff payload: before/after for the fields that changed, with redaction for sensitive values.

[10:49] Kevin Osei: And we have explicit redaction rules—no secrets, no tokens, no API key material. You might still see key “id” or last-4 type metadata, not the secret.

[11:03] Mina Patel: Good.

[11:04] Elena Ruiz: For Splunk, we also care about field names. Like actor.email, actor.type. Are you doing nested JSON?

[11:12] Chloe Martin: It’s structured JSON. Some customers flatten it before Splunk, but we keep it structured. If you ingest JSON in Splunk, it can extract nested fields. For S3 JSONL, it’s just JSON objects per line.

[11:28] Jon Carver: We can handle JSON.

[11:30] Mina Patel: Webhook signing. Do you sign requests?

[11:35] Svetlana Petrenko: We can support HMAC signing: we include a signature header computed over the payload and timestamp, and you verify with a shared secret. We can also include a nonce to prevent replay.

[11:51] Mina Patel: That’s pretty important.

[11:53] Svetlana Petrenko: Yep.

[11:55] Liam O'Rourke: Mina, do you require mTLS or is HMAC okay.

[11:59] Mina Patel: HMAC is okay for start. mTLS would be nice-to-have.

[12:05] Samir Qureshi: And do you log changes to the export configuration itself? Like who enabled export, who changed the webhook URL.

[12:12] Chloe Martin: Yes. Export config changes are also sensitive actions and generate audit events. So “audit_log.export_config.updated” kind of thing.

[12:25] Elena Ruiz: Great.

[12:27] Jon Carver: For S3, what file size do you write? Like one object per minute or what.

[12:33] Svetlana Petrenko: We usually roll files either by time (e.g., every 5 minutes) or size. Again configurable. For high-volume accounts, size-based helps.

[12:47] Jon Carver: And compression is gzip?

[12:49] Svetlana Petrenko: Typically gzip.

[12:51] Jon Carver: Ok.

[12:53] Mina Patel: What about “webhook down” scenario—does it block the rest of your system? Like can it cause latency for the API.

[13:01] Svetlana Petrenko: Good question. No, export is asynchronous. The audit event is emitted and persisted; export happens out-of-band. It shouldn’t add latency to the user request path.

[13:14] Mina Patel: Okay.

[13:16] Elena Ruiz: Metrics. Do you expose exporter metrics? Like, backlog, drop, delay.

[13:23] Svetlana Petrenko: We have dashboards internally and we can share key metrics via the Console: export lag, export error rate, and last successful export timestamp per sink.

[13:35] Chloe Martin: And there are alerts—if export lag exceeds a threshold, we can notify admin emails or webhook a status endpoint. We’re still finalizing what’s self-serve.

[13:49] Jon Carver: I’d want that integrated, like send an alert to PagerDuty.

[13:54] Liam O'Rourke: We can set that up during beta. Also we can provide recommended Grafana-style thresholds, even if you’re not using Grafana.

[14:04] Mina Patel: Okay. Let’s talk about event volume. Roughly, what’s typical? We’re trying to estimate Splunk ingestion cost.

[14:13] Kevin Osei: It varies widely. For most orgs, sensitive actions are relatively low volume compared to app telemetry. Think tens to hundreds per day, but bursts can happen during rollouts or org admin changes.

[14:27] Jon Carver: But you also have model deployment events, right? Like canary start/stop.

[14:31] Kevin Osei: Yes, those are considered sensitive because they affect availability/behavior.

[14:38] Mina Patel: If we only export sensitive actions, that’s manageable.

[14:41] Chloe Martin: Exactly.

[14:44] Elena Ruiz: For Splunk HEC, we also need “sourcetype” set. Do you set that?

[14:50] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes, we can set sourcetype and index fields, depending on your HEC configuration. Usually sourcetype=redwood:audit.

[15:02] Elena Ruiz: Great.

[15:03] Mina Patel: Data residency. We’re in US. But we might expand to EU. If our Redwood deployment is in EU, do the audit logs stay in EU?

[15:13] Kevin Osei: For Private or dedicated regions, we can keep audit log storage and export within that region. For hosted multi-region, it depends on how your org is configured. We can align it to your residency requirements.

[15:30] Jon Carver: For S3 export, we want it to go to a bucket in the same region.

[15:34] Svetlana Petrenko: That’s straightforward.

[15:36] Mina Patel: IP address and user-agent. Do you include that? And what about privacy.

[15:43] Chloe Martin: We include ip and user_agent when available, especially for console and API actions. There are redaction controls; for certain privacy constraints we can truncate or omit parts.

[15:56] Samir Qureshi: Auditors like to see IP.

[15:59] Mina Patel: Security likes to see IP too.

[16:01] Liam O'Rourke: But legal sometimes doesn’t.

[16:03] Kevin Osei: Exactly. We have guidance on retention and redaction; we can set retention policies and export filters.

[16:14] Jon Carver: Okay, can we do both sinks at the same time? Splunk and S3.

[16:20] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes, multiple sinks. Each sink has its own health and retry state.

[16:26] Elena Ruiz: Does that double your load? Like could that cause more lag.

[16:30] Svetlana Petrenko: It can, but we isolate per sink. If Splunk is slow, S3 can still flow.

[16:40] Mina Patel: Great.

[16:42] Jon Carver: One more—do you support Parquet? We prefer Parquet in the lake.

[16:47] Svetlana Petrenko: Not today. It’s JSONL gzip. We’ve heard Parquet requests; it’s on the roadmap, but not in the current beta.

[16:58] Jon Carver: Okay.

[17:00] Mina Patel: Can you walk through a concrete failure scenario? Like Splunk returns 503 for 20 minutes.

[17:08] Svetlana Petrenko: Sure. Exporter attempts delivery, sees 503, backs off. Events continue to be persisted. The exporter maintains a backlog. When Splunk is healthy, we resume and catch up. You’d see increased export lag. If backlog grows too large, we may throttle to avoid overwhelming the sink.

[17:31] Elena Ruiz: And if backlog exceeds some limit?

[17:34] Svetlana Petrenko: Then events go to a dead-letter queue for that sink and we alert. The events are still in the source store, so we can replay.

[17:45] Mina Patel: Okay, so DLQ is per sink. Good.

[17:48] Chloe Martin: Also, the export config can be disabled automatically if it’s continuously failing, to prevent constant retries, but we’d alert and require admin re-enable. That’s configurable.

[18:04] Mina Patel: That’s good. We don’t want infinite noise.

[18:07] Samir Qureshi: For audit, I’d want evidence that the events existed even if export was down.

[18:13] Kevin Osei: Right, that’s where the persisted audit log store and the delivery metrics come in. We can provide an export report if needed.

[18:22] Jon Carver: Another question: Are audit logs accessible via API for us to pull, like if we want to run our own exporter.

[18:30] Chloe Martin: Yes, there is an Audit Logs API to list events with pagination and filters. Access is restricted by RBAC (admin-only by default). Rate limits apply.

[18:44] Jon Carver: That might be our fallback.

[18:47] Elena Ruiz: But pulling from an API at scale is annoying.

[18:50] Jon Carver: True.

[18:52] Mina Patel: This is okay. I think the main open item is Splunk ack. We don’t require it strictly, but we need to document the semantics.

[19:01] Liam O'Rourke: We can document: “delivered means accepted by endpoint.”

[19:05] Mina Patel: Yes.

[19:06] Elena Ruiz: And we’ll de-dup on event_id.

[19:09] Mina Patel: Also, we should see a sample payload. We need to confirm it has actor, target, outcome, timestamp, request id.

[19:17] Chloe Martin: Yep.

[19:19] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll send.

[19:22] Svetlana Petrenko: I can send a couple examples: api_key.rotated, rbac.role.updated with diff, and audit_log.export_config.updated.

[19:34] Mina Patel: Perfect.

[19:36] Jon Carver: Do you include “source” like whether action was via console vs API?

[19:42] Chloe Martin: Yes, there’s a channel/source field. Sometimes called “surface” internally. It indicates console, api, system controller.

[19:52] Jon Carver: Nice.

[19:54] Elena Ruiz: System controller—like automated scaling events?

[19:57] Chloe Martin: Exactly. For example dedicated capacity auto-scaling changes, the actor may be a service identity.

[20:06] Mina Patel: Then, actor attribution: do you show the user who clicked the button when it’s console.

[20:10] Chloe Martin: Yes, actor has type=user and includes user_id and email when available. For service-to-service, actor is type=service.

[20:22] Mina Patel: Great.

[20:24] Liam O'Rourke: We’re about 20 minutes in. Anything else you want to cover—retention tiers, etc.

[20:30] Samir Qureshi: Retention—how long do you keep in your system if we don’t export.

[20:36] Kevin Osei: Default retention depends on plan; we can do longer retention for enterprise. But we usually recommend exporting to your SIEM/lake for your required retention. Internally, we can support 90 days, 180 days, 1 year—depending.

[20:53] Samir Qureshi: Okay.

[20:54] Mina Patel: One subtlety: We need to ensure the export doesn’t include secrets. Like no API keys, no tokens.

[21:01] Kevin Osei: Agreed. Audit payload redaction is strict. You’ll see identifiers and metadata, not secrets. If we ever detect a sensitive key in payload, we scrub it.

[21:13] Mina Patel: Good.

[21:14] Elena Ruiz: Can you include the user-agent? For us, that helps identify automation vs browser.

[21:20] Chloe Martin: Yes.

[21:21] Jon Carver: For S3, do you include a manifest or just objects.

[21:26] Svetlana Petrenko: Just objects. Some customers build a manifest downstream. We can add an optional manifest file but not currently.

[21:37] Jon Carver: Fine.

[21:39] Mina Patel: Okay, I think the rest is just confirm details. I want to talk about throughput—can you handle spikes? Like we do automated provisioning and might generate a lot of events.

[21:50] Svetlana Petrenko: The pipeline is built for bursts. The main constraint is the sink. If Splunk rate limits, we’ll buffer.

[22:01] Mina Patel: What’s the max rate you’ve seen.

[22:05] Svetlana Petrenko: Hard to give a single number; we’ve tested thousands of events per minute. Again, sensitive events are usually far lower.

[22:15] Elena Ruiz: Splunk will rate limit at some point.

[22:17] Svetlana Petrenko: Yep.

[22:19] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, maybe we should switch to next steps. Before that, any final technical questions.

[22:26] Jon Carver: If we choose S3 export, can we still do Splunk via our own pipeline from S3?

[22:32] Mina Patel: We could but it adds delay.

[22:35] Elena Ruiz: Yeah, we want direct for SOC.

[22:38] Jon Carver: Okay.

[22:40] Mina Patel: For beta, I think we want Splunk HEC as primary, and S3 as secondary if possible.

[22:47] Liam O'Rourke: Great. We can do both.

[22:49] Svetlana Petrenko: I’ll need the HEC endpoint, token, and what index/sourcetype you want.

[22:56] Elena Ruiz: We can send that.

[22:58] Mina Patel: And for delivery lag, I’ll go back and confirm our requirement. I think 2 minutes p99 for P0, maybe 5 minutes for the rest.

[23:08] Kevin Osei: That’s a good split.

[23:10] Chloe Martin: Also note, we don’t currently have “priority routing” of exports by event type, but we can talk about whether we can prioritize certain namespaces.

[23:21] Mina Patel: That’d be helpful.

[23:23] Liam O'Rourke: We can capture it as feedback.

[23:26] Svetlana Petrenko: We can also recommend you start with only the P0 sensitive set to keep latency low.

[23:33] Mina Patel: Right.

[23:34] Liam O'Rourke: Okay, I’ll recap action items. Svetlana will send sample payloads and the export options. Chloe will confirm API and rate limits. Kevin will send the reliability and failure-handling writeup. Jon/Elena will send Splunk HEC requirements.

[23:52] Mina Patel: Sounds good.

[23:54] Elena Ruiz: Thanks.

[23:56] Jon Carver: Thanks.

[23:57] Samir Qureshi: Thanks.

[24:00] Liam O'Rourke: Great. We’ll follow up by email and schedule a shorter follow-up next week.

(Transcript continues with additional Q&A and scheduling details; minor crosstalk omitted by Fireflies.)
